title: DEMONS HAVE BETTER THEOLOGY THAN SOME PEOPLE—AND THEY’RE STILL DEMONS
paragraphs: DEMONS HAVE BETTER THEOLOGY THAN SOME PEOPLE—AND THEY’RE STILL DEMONS

They know Jesus is the Son of God. They recognize His authority. They tremble at His name. Yet they remain enemies of God. What if the most terrifying spiritual deception isn't denying that Jesus exists—but knowing exactly who He is while refusing to surrender to Him?
There is a verse in the Bible that should make every churchgoer uncomfortable.
Not because it questions the existence of God.
Not because it attacks Christianity.
But because it exposes something that can hide beneath years of sermons, Bible studies, worship services, ministry involvement, and religious activity.
You can believe everything true about Jesus Christ and still refuse to belong to Him.
And Scripture gives us a disturbing example.
Demons.
Yes. Demons.
They are not atheists.
They do not need archaeological discoveries to convince them Jesus existed.
They do not debate whether He has supernatural authority.
They know.
They recognize Him.
They fear Him.
And they are still demons.
James wrote something that should silence every person who has ever confused religious knowledge with saving faith:
“You believe that God is one. You do well. The demons also believe—and shudder.”
—James 2:19, translated from the Greek
Read that again.
The demons believe.
And they shudder.
But their belief is not repentance. Their recognition is not worshipful surrender. Their knowledge is not reconciliation with God.
Now comes the question that makes this passage painfully personal.
If demons can possess correct theology without possessing saving faith, what makes us think knowing the right answers automatically means our hearts belong to Jesus?
That question is not meant to destroy your assurance in Christ.
It is meant to expose the counterfeit assurance that can keep a person from ever coming to Him.
Because the greatest tragedy is not simply that someone could spend an entire lifetime rejecting Jesus openly.
It is that someone could spend an entire lifetime talking about Jesus, defending Jesus, singing about Jesus, and never truly surrendering to Jesus.
And one day discover that being familiar with the Savior was never the same as being reconciled to Him.
There is something extraordinary buried inside the original Greek of James 2:19.
James begins with the words:
Σὺ πιστεύεις ὅτι εἷς ἐστιν ὁ θεός.
Sy pisteueis hoti heis estin ho theos.
“You believe that God is one.”
This echoes the great confession of Israel found in Deuteronomy 6:4:
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
Shema Yisra'el, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad.
“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.”
This confession was foundational to Israel's worship of the one true God.
James is not mocking that truth. He affirms it.
Believing in the one true God is right.
But then he delivers the devastating comparison.
καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύουσιν καὶ φρίσσουσιν.
Kai ta daimonia pisteuousin kai phrissousin.
“And the demons believe—and shudder.”
The Greek verb φρίσσουσιν (phrissousin) conveys trembling or shuddering in fear.
James is making a piercing argument: correct belief about God, by itself, is not proof of a living, obedient faith.
He is not saying demons have complete or superior theology in every respect.
They do not.
Their understanding is corrupted by rebellion, and their response to God is not the trusting love of redeemed children.
But they know certain truths that many people deny.
And that makes the comparison so frightening.
Because there are people who recognize the existence of God without ever submitting to His authority.
People who can explain salvation while resisting the Savior.
People who know the language of repentance but have spent years defending the very sins they refuse to abandon.
People who can identify false teaching in someone else's life while refusing to confront the pride growing inside their own.
And before you imagine somebody else while reading those words, consider the possibility that Scripture is inviting you to examine yourself.
Not your pastor.
Not the person who offended you.
Not the Christian who disappointed you.
You.
Because religious deception becomes most dangerous when we are certain it could never happen to us.
Consider what happened when Jesus encountered a man tormented by demons in the region of the Gerasenes.
The man was living among tombs.
His life had become a picture of isolation, torment, and destruction.
People had tried to restrain him.
Chains could not hold him.
Human strength could not restore him.
He lived surrounded by death, crying out and injuring himself.
Then Jesus arrived.
And the spiritual powers tormenting that man immediately recognized the One standing before them.
In Mark 5:7, the cry comes:
“What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?”
They knew His identity.
They recognized His authority.
They understood that they could not treat Him as an ordinary man.
And yet they were not His disciples.
They were His enemies.
Do you see the distinction?
Recognizing the authority of Jesus is not the same as lovingly submitting to Jesus.
The demons knew who stood before them.
But they did not love Him.
They did not repent.
They did not become obedient followers.
And the man they had tormented desperately needed something they could never give him.
Deliverance.
Restoration.
A new life.
That is exactly what Jesus brought.
Later in the same account, the formerly tormented man is found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
The man who had lived among the tombs was no longer defined by the place where everyone expected him to remain.
Jesus had stepped into his devastation and rewritten the story.
And here is something worth remembering.
The demons recognized Jesus.
But the delivered man wanted to follow Him.
One response was terror before authority.
The other was the beginning of a transformed life.
That difference matters.
Because Christianity is not merely the ability to make accurate statements about Christ.
It is being brought to God through Christ.
It is receiving His grace through faith.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
It is the beginning of a new life that His Spirit continues to transform.
Not perfection.
Not sinlessness.
Not an impressive religious résumé.
A genuine relationship with the living Lord that bears fruit because His grace is at work.
And that brings us to one of the most sobering statements Jesus ever made.
In Matthew 7:21–23, Jesus warns that not everyone who calls Him “Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven.
Some will point to astonishing religious activity performed in His name.
They will appeal to what they said.
What they did.
What appeared to happen through their ministry.
But Jesus describes a terrible reality.
There can be outward religious activity without a genuine relationship with Him.
And the words at the center of His warning are devastating:
“I never knew you.”
—Matthew 7:23
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say, “You never attended enough services.”
He does not say, “You never collected enough Bible knowledge.”
He does not say, “You failed to build an impressive ministry.”
His warning exposes the absence of a genuine relationship with Him, alongside a life characterized by lawlessness.
That should sober us.
But we must read this passage carefully.
Jesus is not teaching that genuine believers earn salvation through flawless obedience.
He is not saying a struggling Christian who sincerely trusts Him will be rejected because of weakness, tears, or repeated battles with sin.
Scripture teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the very next verse says that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
The order matters.
We are not saved because we have successfully transformed ourselves.
We are saved by Christ, and His grace begins transforming us.
Good works are not the purchase price of salvation.
They are the fruit of a faith made alive by God's grace.
James is confronting a faith that exists only as a claim, never expressing itself in mercy or obedience.
Paul is confronting the idea that sinners can earn justification through their works.
They are not contradicting one another.
They are exposing two different errors.
Paul tells us that we cannot save ourselves.
James tells us that living faith is not merely an empty profession.
And both point us away from self-reliance and toward Jesus Christ.
But perhaps this is where the article stops being theological and starts becoming personal.
Because some of us have learned how to sound spiritually healthy while quietly falling apart.
We know which Bible verses to post.
We know how to say “God is good” when somebody asks how we are doing.
We know how to encourage other people.
We know how to pray in public.
But behind closed doors, there are battles nobody sees.
The resentment we keep feeding.
The secret habit we keep excusing.
The bitterness we call discernment.
The pride we disguise as spiritual maturity.
The dishonesty we justify because telling the truth might cost us something.
The unforgiveness we have allowed to become part of our identity.
And sometimes the most exhausting part is not the struggle itself.
It is the effort of maintaining an image that says we have no struggle at all.
You can know the Greek word for repentance and still be terrified to confess your sin.
You can explain grace beautifully while believing that God could never forgive what you have done.
You can defend the authority of Scripture while quietly resisting the very command God is bringing to your attention.
You can tell everyone that Jesus changes lives while secretly wondering whether He can still change yours.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Not because you need another argument about demons.
But because something inside you is tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of knowing the right words without experiencing the honesty those words require.
Tired of carrying guilt into worship and taking it home again.
Tired of promising God that tomorrow will be different, only to discover that willpower alone cannot rescue the human heart.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Jesus did not come merely to make you better at appearing religious. He came to save sinners.
That is the Gospel.
Not that you are good enough to impress God.
Not that you can repair your past through religious activity.
Not that your public reputation can compensate for your private rebellion.
Christ came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).
He lived the righteous life we could not live.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And because He lives, forgiveness is not an empty religious slogan.
Redemption is not wishful thinking.
New life is not reserved for people whose past looks respectable.
The cross tells us that sin is far more serious than we wanted to admit.
The resurrection tells us that Jesus is far more powerful than our sin.
And grace tells us that the door of mercy is opened by the Savior, not by our ability to deserve Him.
Think about Peter.
Peter knew Jesus personally.
He heard His teaching.
He witnessed His miracles.
He declared that Jesus was the Christ.
And then, on the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The third denial was followed by the crowing of a rooster.
And Luke tells us that Peter went outside and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
Imagine that moment.
The man who had promised loyalty now carried the memory of his own cowardice.
The disciple who had spoken so confidently had discovered how weak he really was.
He had the right confession.
But he had failed terribly when faithfulness became costly.
And yet his failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ asked him three times whether he loved Him.
Three questions.
Three opportunities to answer.
And with those questions came a renewed commission to care for Christ's sheep.
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial never happened.
He restored a fallen disciple and entrusted him with responsibility.
That is grace.
Not grace that declares betrayal harmless.
Grace that confronts failure and restores the repentant.
Grace that does not leave a broken person chained forever to the worst night of his life.
Peter's story was not rewritten because Peter suddenly became impressive.
It was rewritten because the risen Jesus was merciful.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the most extraordinary part is that Jesus is still doing the work of redemption.
Not by excusing sin.
Not by celebrating rebellion.
Not by lowering the holiness of God.
But by calling sinners to repentance and offering the forgiveness He purchased through His blood.
There is another Greek word worth understanding.
μετάνοια — metanoia.
Repentance.
The word refers to a change of mind, and in biblical usage it involves a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because somebody discovered what you did.
It is not merely crying because consequences have arrived.
It is not negotiating with God so that you can keep the sin and escape the judgment.
Repentance is turning to God with a changed heart and mind, acknowledging that His ways are right and that we need His mercy.
And even here, we depend upon grace.
We cannot manufacture spiritual life by sheer determination.
God calls us to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15), and His kindness leads us toward repentance (Romans 2:4).
Which means that the conviction you feel while reading Scripture should not automatically be mistaken for God pushing you away.
His Word may be exposing what needs to be brought into the light.
And the answer is not to hide more carefully.
It is to come to Christ.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe people know what happened.
Maybe your name became attached to a mistake, a betrayal, an addiction, or a decision that shattered relationships.
Or maybe your scandal is invisible.
Nobody knows how cold your heart has become.
Nobody knows how long you have carried jealousy.
Nobody knows how much you have compromised.
Nobody knows how often you have smiled while feeling spiritually empty.
But Jesus knows.
And this is where the Gospel becomes astonishing.
The One who knows the truth about your sin is the very One who calls sinners to come to Him for mercy.
He is not deceived by religious performance.
He cannot be manipulated by impressive words.
He does not need your carefully edited testimony.
He calls you to come truthfully.
Confess what is wrong.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Trust what He accomplished through His death and resurrection.
And follow Him.
Not because following Him will always be comfortable.
But because no other Savior can give eternal life.
In John 6:68, Peter asked Jesus:
“Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life.”
That is the question every exhausted soul eventually has to face.
Where else will you go?
Back to the sin that promised freedom and produced bondage?
Back to the approval of people who cannot cleanse your conscience?
Back to religious activity that helps you avoid dealing honestly with God?
Back to the belief that one more achievement will finally make you worthy?
Or will you come to Jesus?
The Jesus who welcomed the repentant tax collector.
The Jesus who restored Peter.
The Jesus who promised paradise to a dying criminal who turned to Him in faith.
The Jesus who bore our sins and rose victorious over death.
The Jesus who still calls the weary to Himself.
And here is the distinction that changes everything.
Demons believe Jesus is powerful.
Saving faith entrusts itself to Jesus as Savior and Lord.
Demons recognize His identity.
Believers are called to love Him, trust Him, and follow Him.
Demons tremble before His authority.
Those reconciled to God can approach Him through Christ with confidence in His mercy.
Not because they are stronger than demons.
Not because their knowledge is more impressive.
But because Jesus saves.
This is why the Christian life cannot be reduced to winning theological arguments.
Sound doctrine matters deeply.
Truth matters.
The deity of Christ matters.
His bodily resurrection matters.
The Gospel must not be distorted.
But doctrine was never meant to become a trophy that allows us to admire our knowledge while neglecting the God who revealed Himself.
Theology should lead us toward worship, humility, love, repentance, and obedience.
If studying Scripture makes us increasingly arrogant, cruel, dishonest, and unteachable, something is wrong with the way we are responding to what we know.
First Corinthians 8:1 warns that knowledge can puff up, while love builds up.
That does not make knowledge unnecessary.
It means knowledge without love can become a weapon in the hands of pride.
And perhaps one of the saddest sights in Christianity is a person who can dismantle somebody else's doctrinal error in minutes but cannot bring themselves to say three simple words.
“I was wrong.”
Or two even harder words.
“Forgive me.”
Some people can explain the doctrine of grace but refuse to extend grace.
Some can preach about holiness while secretly making peace with sin.
Some can quote the words of Jesus while treating people in ways that contradict His commands.
And every one of us needs to remain humble enough to ask whether that contradiction has found a home in our own hearts.
Not because every inconsistency proves someone is unsaved.
Christians still struggle.
Christians still stumble.
Christians still need correction, confession, and forgiveness.
But there is a profound difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
Between falling and refusing to get up.
Between confessing wrongdoing and continually defending it.
The evidence of grace is not that a Christian never needs repentance.
It is that the Christian life becomes one of continually returning to Christ in faith and repentance.
And if you are reading this while feeling deeply convicted, please do not turn this article into another reason to despair.
Look at the Savior.
First John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive and cleanse us.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And John 6:37 contains a promise that should be precious to every person afraid of being rejected:
“The one who comes to me, I will in no way throw out.”
Jesus does not promise that following Him will require no change.
He promises that those who come to Him will not be cast away.
That is where your hope belongs.
Not in the intensity of your emotions.
Not in the number of tears you cry.
Not in how convincingly you can describe your spiritual experiences.
In Christ.
His finished work.
His resurrection.
His faithfulness.
His mercy.
And His power to make all things new.
Maybe tonight you need to stop asking whether you know enough about Jesus and start asking whether you are actually trusting Him.
Maybe you need to confess something.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you wounded.
Maybe you need to walk away from a compromise you have been protecting.
Maybe you need to stop performing spiritual strength and finally tell a trusted believer that you need prayer.
Or maybe you have been avoiding Jesus because you believe your past has placed you beyond His reach.
Remember Peter.
Remember the criminal beside the cross.
Remember the man who once lived among the tombs.
Remember that the Gospel is not a story about flawless people finding a religion that congratulates them.
It is the announcement that the holy Son of God came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
And that rescue is not something we purchase with money, religious service, or moral accomplishments.
It is the gift of God's grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
So if you have never truly turned to Him, do not settle for knowing facts about Him.
Come to Him.
And if you already belong to Him but have been hiding in shame, return to the light.
Tell Him the truth.
You do not need a theatrical prayer.
You need an honest heart before the living God.
You can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I believe You are the Son of God, that You died for my sins, and that You rose again. I confess that I have sinned against You. I have sometimes been more concerned with appearing faithful than actually obeying You. Forgive me. Teach me genuine repentance. I cannot save myself. I place my trust in Your grace and Your finished work. Change my heart. Lead me in Your truth. Help me love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. Let my life bear witness that You are not merely someone I know about, but the Savior and Lord I trust. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects what is happening in your heart, do not let the moment disappear beneath another scroll.
Take the next faithful step.
Open your Bible.
Speak to a mature Christian who can walk alongside you.
Become part of a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and believers care for one another.
Seek reconciliation where possible.
And remember that spiritual growth is not measured by how impressive you appear tomorrow.
It is measured over time by a life increasingly shaped by the grace and truth of Jesus Christ.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell access to God.
But to keep bringing biblical truth into a world filled with distraction, confusion, spiritual exhaustion, and countless voices competing for the human heart.
There are people who will never walk into a church building but may read a Scripture-centered article shared by a friend.
There are believers who are struggling quietly and need to be reminded of the promises of God.
There are families who need encouragement to open the Bible together.
There are people whose understanding of Christianity has been shaped by hypocrisy, disappointment, or misinformation, who deserve to hear the actual Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And there are Christians who are hungry to grow beyond inspirational quotations into deeper biblical understanding.
We want those resources to remain accessible to people who need them.
We want to keep creating Christ-centered articles, biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship materials that help people return to Scripture and grow in their walk with Jesus.
But meaningful ministry takes time, work, and resources.
Not because a monthly payment earns His favor.
You glorify God by trusting and obeying Christ. Supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one voluntary expression of that love.
Scripture encourages believers to give willingly and cheerfully, not reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And it recognizes the value of supporting those who faithfully labor in Gospel ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14; Galatians 6:6).
If you already give to your local church, please continue to honor those responsibilities as you prayerfully discern your generosity.
It is simply an opportunity to help sustain and expand the work.
To help more people encounter biblical truth.
To help more struggling believers find encouragement rooted in Scripture.
To help make discipleship resources more accessible.
To stand alongside a mission that seeks to point people beyond personalities, platforms, and religious performance to Jesus Christ Himself.
They are a small expression of gratitude to those who choose to help carry it forward.

If Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you through a difficult season, or reminded you that Jesus has not finished His work in your life, consider joining us as a monthly supporter.
Not merely to increase numbers.
Somebody may be attending church while privately wondering whether God could ever forgive them.
Somebody may be defending Christianity publicly while slowly drifting away from Christ privately.
And somebody may be one honest conversation away from admitting that they need the Savior they have spent years talking about.
And if this message exposed something in your heart, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not have to reveal private details publicly. A simple request is enough for fellow believers to know you would welcome prayer.
And if God has restored you after a season of failure, consider sharing a brief testimony that honors Christ. Your story may encourage someone who believes their own failure must be the end.
Because the world does not need more Christians who are merely impressive at sounding Christian.
It needs the faithful witness of people who have encountered the mercy of Jesus and are learning to live in His truth.
People who know that salvation is by grace.
People who take sin seriously without pretending to be sinless.
People who speak truth without abandoning love.
People who can say, “I was wrong,” because they no longer need to build their identity on being right about everything.
People who can extend forgiveness because they know how much they have been forgiven.
People whose lives make the Gospel visible, not because they are perfect, but because they keep pointing back to the perfect Savior.
And now, one final thought.
The demons in the Gospels recognized Jesus when He stood before them.
They knew His authority.
They feared His power.
They could not deny who He was.
But their knowledge did not make them His followers.
So do not let your confidence rest merely in the fact that you know the right religious answers.
Ask yourself what you are doing with the truth you know.
Is it leading you toward Jesus?
Is it humbling you?
Is it awakening love for God and others?
Is it calling you to repent where you have compromised?
Is it teaching you to depend more deeply upon His grace?
Because one day, your theological vocabulary will not be your Savior.
Your ministry achievements will not be your Savior.
Your reputation will not be your Savior.
Your social media following will not be your Savior.
Your financial contributions will not be your Savior.
Jesus Christ alone is the Savior.
And the good news is that He does not merely offer you information about Himself.
He offers Himself.
His mercy.
His forgiveness.
His righteousness.
His life.
The One who died and rose again is worthy of more than our acknowledgment.
He is worthy of our trust, our love, our worship, and our lives.
And if your story is filled with things you wish you could undo, remember that the risen Christ is not limited by the chapter you are ashamed to remember.
He does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely more wonderful.
He saves sinners.
He restores the repentant.
He makes the dead alive.
And He writes grace into stories that once seemed hopeless.
The most terrifying thing is to know who Jesus is and never come to Him. The most beautiful thing is that, even now, He calls sinners to come.
